en: The Sanskrit language of the Western Heaven originates from the *dhāraṇī* of the Tripitaka.

Thus, with the rise of the Image-Teaching (the Mahāyāna), the Sanskrit was translated into the language of Tang, taking vocal sound as a Buddha-work (*buddhakārya*). As for what the Tiantai Master Zhiyi transmitted, it has become most prevalent in the Eastern Land;
indeed, this single method of *nienfo* (Buddha-recollection) opens up myriad ways of transformation, much like the praise of Śākyamuni in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.

Master Yuán’s contemplation of Amitābha and his eulogy of the Buddha’s merits to propagate them on behalf of the Buddha were nothing other than swift weapons for benefiting humans and devas and delivering them from birth and death.
Because Master Gāoshēng possessed a nature as keen and enlightened as the celestial realm and a mastery of the meanings of the scriptures, he compiled Buddhist texts into bound volumes;
rather than keeping these for himself, he sought to broaden the authentic transmission so that later students might obtain them.
His establishment [of this work] allows one to deeply penetrate the stage of an *ācārya*. This master’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) are thus extensively applied.
Some may say that Peak (Gao Feng) is a veteran of the monastic community;
while this book is indeed beautiful, the Buddha cannot be seen through physical form nor sought through sound. Yet now, having set aside the fruit of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), he employs...
Regarding the mind's engagement with the causes of outflows (*sāsrava*), I fear that the Buddha-dharma may not be fully exhausted therein. Alas!
Within the realms transformed by the ten billion emanation bodies, [the Buddha] connects with the various capacities of sentient beings according to their faculties and types.

These eighty-four thousand gates of perfect penetration—each gate being a path to liberation—depend ultimately upon the nature of one’s own spiritual capacity. Even an ordinary person or a pauper, provided they can undergo threefold incense-baths and once...
To praise it once and extol it: as soon as one opens the mouth to recite the Buddha’s name, the lotus has already been planted in the pond of the Pure Land.

Indeed, there are those who state that by uttering the Name ten times, one is reborn in the Buddha-field. If this were the teaching of a fool, how could it deceive me? I, the Fool, request to cite this as a refutation for those who harbor doubts.
On the third day before the Shangji festival of the Dinghai year of the Zhizyuan era, the Dharma Master Lingbao, who also practiced the six supernatural powers,
performed the ritual services for the bequeathed teachings.

*The Recorded Sayings of Master Yin of Longquan Monastery on Gaofeng Mountain*,
Compiled by the Junior Disciple Ruying, Abbot of the Sixth Patriarch’s Monastery. Compiled by De Yin,
the Dharma-transmitting Bhikṣu and Eleventh Abbot of Longquan Monastery on Gaofeng Mountain, who has humbly received [this honor].
As a son of the Śākya, I have the honor of dwelling in the Brahma-palace. I receive the imperial decree of the Sovereign Emperor, which is no light matter;

I am moved by the compassionate grace of my Master, which is truly profound. Having cast off all worldly attachments, the Mind-Seal has been transmitted to me alone. I strictly observe the pure regulations and diligently study the yellow scrolls.
The Dharma teachings are vast and deep, expansive and boundless; the Buddha-gate is magnificent and sublime. Although it is said that there is—

The measure [of this work] is boundless; one must thoroughly investigate its doctrines and its underlying intent. Since the surviving instructions have long been rife with errors and corruptions, who has exerted the effort to rectify them?
Although even those of humble monastic standing lack such skill, I venture to contribute my own editorial labor. Regarding Buddhist rites, I have pruned the redundant and extracted the essentials;
regarding ritual protocols, I have followed the old while adding what was new. Though the practices employed by the various regions differ according to local customs, [I have harmonized them...]

It is indeed extraordinary. Yet, as the world shares a common script, there is nothing that cannot be applied. Should you deign to examine this, it would be a great fortune if you were to exercise your editorial judgment.
[The following is the inscription for] the *Lichun* (Beginning of Spring) Gate in the *Shujing* (Scripture of the Altar).

At this time, the *tiaofeng* breeze stirs gently as the virtue of Wood begins its circuit. The imperial carriage solemnly awaits at the eastern outskirts; the *xian* pipes send forth the first ash in the vermilion chamber.
The earthen ox is brought forth to prognosticate auspicious signs, and colored swallows are adorned to welcome fortune.

As prosperity arrives and adversity reaches its end, plants and trees glow with renewed luster; as the old is discarded and the new established, mountains and rivers take on a transformed appearance. Withered roots and parched trunks catch the warmth.
The vital energy (*qi*) begins its sprouting; those in hibernation and the hidden-scaled creatures awaken upon encountering the harmony of Yang.

The three hundred and sixty days of the Yao calendar mark the very commencement of this season, and among the nine categories of the *Ji Chou*, there is none that does not advocate for cultivation and reverence. Thus, we establish this Dharma assembly.
The lush foliage welcomes the evening light;
again, the Three Yangs begin to peak. All phenomena flourish as the golden gates see the reed-pipes stir with rising ash, and the grain-tubes at the valley mouth turn back.

The *Taicou* [musical note] vibrates; the east wind melts the frost as a day of harmonious vital energy disperses over towers and terraces. At dawn, mists coalesce into fragrance, and auspicious light floats upon the grasses and trees.
Calamities depart with the waning year, while blessings follow the arrival of early spring. With the green ritual jade, one should reverently attend to the rites of the East;
the elaborate ceremonies ought to be cultivated in the West [India].
In the first month, the Feng calendar opens a new beginning; the dragon’s strides change the sequence of the seasons. The diagrams of Fu Xi harmonize with the three yang lines to achieve great peace;

the *Spring Annals* of the *Lunyu* rectify the five beginnings to record the arrival of spring. Wild plum blossoms scatter their powder as the winter snows first melt; the imperial willows sway their golden threads in the east wind.

The great breath of the universe fans forth warmth as the divine artificer operates its subtle mechanism; the cold of Yan Valley is withdrawn and the vital energy of life fully returns to the sprouting buds.

Joyfully we encounter the beginning of the year, a time when the main gate welcomes a hundred blessings; with delight we exercise our sincere hearts at the commencement of the assembly of the myriad spirits.

Furthermore, as the cycle of the stars has returned and the first month of spring has arrived, we observe the conjunction of the two luminaries; the *Taicou* note accords with the laws of the three yang energies.

The eastern wind touches all things, causing the sand to sprout and tender grasses to unfurl anew in green. The morning sun brings forth warmth, its light falling upon the small paths between the lanes.
The peach blossoms are still faintly rosy. We have selected an auspicious day of the grain-planting season to reverently pour forth our humble sincerity.

Furthermore, as the year’s cycle begins to change and the month’s auspiciousness first brings harmony, it is precisely the time when the Azure Dragon manifests its form, coinciding with the Blue Bird presiding over the opening of spring.
Preface: Ten-li of towers and pavilions add to the refined air; a thousand homes with their curtained windows lock in auspicious mists.
Reverently facing the new sun, we devoutly perform Buddhist rites on this New Year’s Day.

The preface deduces the five beginnings; the calendar rectifies the three primal sources. We raise our cups to offer the inscription upon the cypress leaves, and present the hymn of the pepper blossoms to pray for longevity.
Within the beast-shaped wine vessels, the celestial brew overflows with its concentrated fragrance; at the doorways, the chicken-shaped talismans remain silent as the baleful omens withdraw.
This is the day when the myriad people don their peach-bark garments; it is the morning when the Emperor of the Nine Palaces prays for a bountiful harvest.

On the first day of the New Year, the lanterns shine brilliantly at a thousand gates; the lutes and songs resound through the nine thoroughfares. In the immortal grottoes, peach blossoms cluster like brocade;
by the imperial moat, fresh willows sway with golden hues. The bright moon bathes the stern city walls, adorning the splendor of the imperial capital; fragrant breezes pierce the forbidden precincts.
The streets display the splendor of the imperial capital. At the watchtowers, the jade water-chimes fall silent; on the Qin roads, the golden seal-paste is still wet.
The Star Bridge opens its iron chains, and the Fire Trees join their silver blossoms. Thus we extend our humble sincerity in celebration and welcome a hundred converging blessings.

Furthermore, as the first month of spring reached its midpoint, the frozen ice had already melted. Five-phoenix clouds descended from mid-air to support the imperial carriage; six giant tortoises emerged from the sea to carry the mountain.
Wherever the Milky Way was cloudless, the sounds of pipes and songs boiled over like a cauldron; wherever the moon shone upon the jeweled eaves, every household was filled with joy.
The wind is gentle through the curtains; the lamps shine with beauty throughout the thousand gates at night. For ten li, silks and brocades abound in the splendor of spring.
What auspicious karmic conditions! What a propitious season! What great merit! What grand adornment!
It is the second month;

the Azure Dragon is at the head of the sequence, and the Dark Bird presides over the division of the seasons. It is the very beginning of the "Treading upon the Ground" in the *Feng* (Air) of the *Bin*, and the day when the Zhou regulations dictate the opening of the ice storehouse.
The swallows' chatter is half-harmonious, while the orioles' song is artful; the fragrance of flowers mingles with the clear scent of the grasses. The warmth of spring abounds.
Vivid and bright, the myriad phenomena give birth to spring; the Dharma assembly is solemnly cultivated as a single heart of sincerity returns to the Buddha.
Furthermore, peach cheeks glow in the dawn, willow eyes peer into the spring; a misty, fine rain wets the fragrant dust, and a light, auspicious smoke wafts through the air.
The warm valley is bathed in sunlight, as the mountain colors brew an air of harmony that mingles with the brows of the peaks;

the wind plays with the fragrance of flowers, coalescing into a splendor of spring that bewilders the eye’s horizon. In the imperial gardens, the orioles warble with artistry; in the painted halls, the swallow colonies have newly returned.

At the Cold Food Festival, the elm trees gather the lingering rain; from the mulberry and hackberry groves, a cold mist rises. Flower-litters vie for elegance with fresh adornments; they exchange wheat porridge to preserve ancient custom.
In a thousand homes, fire is forbidden as vermilion trays present the auspicious sign of painted ducks; along the nine thoroughfares, there is no dust as embroidered [carriages] pass.
In the courtyard, the game of fighting cocks was being staged, just as we encountered this auspicious season. I wish to pour forth my sincere heart:

on the third day of the month, when the moon traverses the mansion of Wei (Gwei), the musical pitch is tuned to Guxi (Gu-xin). Benevolent breezes blow harmoniously, scattering the remaining petals of peach blossoms and adorning them with their lingering fragrance.
The rain falls in a misty drizzle, soaking through the colors of a thousand layers of willows. In the swallow’s tower, all is silent;
in the courtyard of floating willow catkins, the days drag on. The *xiqi* ducks bathe in the bright river; the cuckoo cries under the night moon.

Furthermore, the rain has cleared from the elm buds, and the waves have warmed with the peach blossoms. Deep shade gradually obscures the four directions, and the splendor of spring has already passed by one-third.
The red apricots are seductive, lightly emitting smokeless fire; the green willows are supple and drooping, yet remain without cocoons.
The swallow returns to its nest, busily seeking mud; the bee flaps its wings upward, hurriedly clinging to the cotton-floss.

On Qingming, peach blossoms toss crimson waves upon the water, and duckweed spreads green across the ponds. Palace ladies pass the candles as the blue smoke drifts into the vermilion gates. The fire-drills...
The yews are drilled for firewood as cold flames newly arise upon the purple roads; willow catkins fly wildly across the surface of the water, and paulownia blossoms dot the tips of the branches.
Having encountered this auspicious season, I briefly extend my sincere devotion.

The Upper Ji festival has just passed, and the second seasonal marker, the Double-Three, is observed once more. At the winding *qu-shui* (curved waters) of the Eastern Hall, the gentle breeze of the Southern Ford blows harmoniously.
Amidst the fragrance of red apricots, they vie in playing *chū-jù*; beneath the shade of green willows, they emerge with the grace of autumn waters. The wind is light over the banks of the Yi River.

I listened to the youths chanting their hymns at the ritual of the rain altar. At Lanling, where the bamboos flourished, the assembly of worthies laid out their banquet for the *xiuji* purification rite.

In the fourth month, the "grain autumn" (*maiqiu*), the air was invigorating; in the summer of the *huai* trees, the breeze was clear. Amidst the deep green of the pond, the sword-like leaves of the *pu* grass thrust open through the three-foot water, scattering in wild profusion.
In the crimson paths, mossy coins purchase half a measure of spring. Early cicadas break into intermittent, throat-choking new notes;
nursing swallows warble their clever, melodic calls. Just as we face this clear and harmonious month, we extend our solemn and pure sincerity.

Furthermore, the Azure Emperor (Qinghuang) unravels the seal-script, and the Red Lord (Chidi) presides over the balance. Young bamboo shoots grow into poles, swaying the azure tassels within the carriage;
round lotus leaves float upon the water, cast like full pools of green coins. As the strings of Shun’s lute are first plucked amidst the warm breeze, the *ban* fans are suddenly [set aside].
Swinging in the bright moonlight, the yellow oriole seeks its old friend; the purple swallow leads forth its new fledglings.

In the fifth month, the wind blows fragrant along the banks of Chu, and the air at Lake Jian is cool and refreshing. The plum rains have just ceased, and wondrous clouds rise toward the peaks beyond the vast horizons. The *huai* trees—
Shaded from the slow passage of time, one fears the sun scorching the void; ten *li* away, the green lotuses are fragrant and rich, while by the two windows, the green bamboo is pure and elegant.
Midsummer has duly arrived, and the Dharma assembly is now brilliantly inaugurated.
Furthermore, as the sun traverses the mansion of East Well (Jing), the Dipper points toward the south. Lotus leaves sway with the wind like round green parasols;
pomegranate flowers reflect the sunlight, forming clusters of crimson headscarves. At the court of Yu, the lute that dispels resentment is played; in the palace of Tang, verses are chanted.
The phrase "giving rise to coolness" [describes how] the chirping of cicadas and the movement of grasshoppers accord with the seasons, fulfilling the natural sentiments of all things.
Dwelling in a swallow’s nest or a snail’s shell, one may exalt the sublime matters of the Buddha-fruit. On the fifth day of the fifth month...
Green mugwort hangs from the gates; the yellow plum season has ended with the rains. The people of Chu offer sacrifices to Qu Yuan, skillfully winding silk threads;

the customs of Han worship Chen Gong, all clad in pure garments. Silken banners are raised where dragon boats compete amidst the clamor of drums; painted barges return as the sound of ivory clappers fills the air with laughter and conversation.
Fortunate to encounter this auspicious festival of the Center of Heaven, we reverently welcome the Compassionate Honored One of the Ocean Assembly.
Furthermore, the rain has ceased at the southern window; the lake on the eastern bank is calm. In ten thousand homes, peach and willow branches hang from their gates;

for ten li, lotus and water-lily leaves rise high like canopies over the water. Jade wrists bind flower-patterned snake-cord bracelets; ice-like skin is draped in tiger-shirted mugwort garments. A new moon hangs in the sky.
A single precious mirror first opens its case; bright stars reflect in the water like several panels of pearl curtains before the hooks are drawn.

Amidst cloud-peaks emerging from the crags in the sixth month, a fire-parasol spreads across the sky. Within the fragrance of red lotuses, the pavilions and terraces by the pond are free of even a speck of vulgarity—how pure!

Where the spring water resounds, the pine gates and bamboo thickets naturally grow cool; fish leap and their fins stir the green lotuses, while cicadas drag out their lingering cries from the verdant willows.
Half of the year’s passage of time has already elapsed; thus, the teachings of the Sixfold Perfection are humbly cultivated.

Furthermore, the *Linzhong* pipe renews the ancient pitch-pipes, while the *Liuchou* lunar mansion verifies the new celestial coordinates. As the scorching sun melts metal, it marks the first retreat of the *Gengjin* (Metal) phase;
as the drought clouds sear like fire, one knows that the *Dahuo* (Great Fire) constellation is about to move westward. Spot by spot, the stains moisten my breast-cloth; the brilliance—

The fierce heat of summer assails our pillows and mats; from the small coves, red lotuses bring forth a succession of exquisite, fragrant scents, while along the winding banks, green willows cast shifting, sparse shadows of pale light.
Faced with such a season, it is fitting to establish a *dharmapūjā* site.
In the seventh month, the handle of the Big Dipper points toward the west, and the sun travels through the southern path. As the accumulated rains clear, the *bānshàn* fans are gradually set aside;

as a fresh coolness arises, the *hándēng* lamps may be drawn near. Drizzling jade dew drops onto golden platters, and the light, expansive golden wind stirs within the jade palace. The lotuses on the islets—

Fragrant incense scatters like a few stars of fireflies as they pierce the curtains; the willows along the embankment have withdrawn their mist, and the single-threaded chirping of cicadas enters the ears.
Now that we have arrived at this pure season, the Dharma assembly is opened with radiant splendor.
Furthermore, as the God of Gold (Kubera) holds his staff, a cool breeze arises within the jade palace. At the window facing Han, the lamp-light has already touched my heart;

in the state of Wu, the water-millets and fresh perch stir my inspiration all the more. Beneath the leaves of the paulownia trees, the evening wind whistles and reports the arrival of autumn; atop the tips of the willow branches, the morning dew falls.
The rapids urge the departure of summer; fortunately, we encounter the pure radiance of autumn. It is fitting to establish wholesome causes.

As the Seventh Night of the Seventh Month marks the beginning of the ninefold autumnal season, and the festival arrives, Hao Sheng once displayed the books within his belly, while Lady Ruan extensively spread her offerings across the courtyard.
The outer brocade: the moon rises in the jade-like sky, its crescent high-hanging like a slender silver hook;
dew drips onto the golden platter, densely arrayed as fine droplets of pearls. The two stars meet in the Milky Way; at midnight, the Jade Cord descends low.

This is precisely the auspicious occasion of the heavens, what is called a most excellent night for the human world. Having fortunately encountered this noble season, one should cultivate virtuous causes.

The Mid-Autumn Festival of the first month of autumn has arrived at the full moon. The central solar term divides its governance; the crescent moon is now perfectly round, its shimmering cold light truly unconventional.
The golden breeze fans gently, and a piercing, refreshing coolness arises of its own accord. Tugao leaves drift yellow, and reed flowers fly white. It is precisely fitting for this honor.
This is the day of the Buddha Dipamkara’s illumination, the time when the Earth Official pardons transgressions.

In the eighth month, the *lü* (pitch-pipe) is tuned to Nanlü; the imperial decree is solemn in the Western Palace. Tufts of reed flowers cover the marshes, and the leaves of the trees rustle as they flutter down.

In the courtyards, the wind carries the sound of several plaintive trumpet calls that break the heart with sorrow; from neighboring watchtowers, ten thousand pestles of cold mortars ring out, adding to the resentment of parting.
The bamboo washes away a thousand drops of jade maidens' tears; the lotus petals turn like Xi Shi’s six-zhu robe.

Furthermore, the rains have ceased and the sky has cleared; the wind off the floating duckweed heralds a refreshing coolness. In the crystalline heavens, the star-spoon points toward the month of You (August-September); on this auspicious night, the earthen drums already welcome the onset of cold.
The radiance of the waters merges with the light of the heavens; the chirping of crickets mingles with the rhythmic sound of the wooden pestle. Rock oaks reflect their brilliance against the window.
The fragrant essence has successively conveyed celestial incense; the lotus flowers, intoxicated by the sun, appear tender and soft in their fresh adornment like the beauty of a kingdom.
Mid-autumn marks the halfway point of the three autumns; the hundred *kṣaṇas* are evenly divided. Upon the clouds, the precious moon is perfectly round; upon the water, the pearl-like stars twinkle.
Brilliant! The dew is thick and the shadows of the *wú* trees grow faint; the breeze is gentle and the fragrance of the *guì* trees floats forth.
Half-plant, half-real, wild geese in the sky form rows like embroidered characters; flickering on and off, the fisherman’s fires by the river shine like the constellations.
Furthermore, the golden stalks hold dew, and the jade pavilions are free of dust. The white moon arrives; within the brilliance of the precious mirror, not a speck of obscuration remains.

As drifting clouds are gathered in, the Jade Tower stands high, its coldness unbearable. The sound of the flute resonates across the mountain passes, mingling with the chime of the water-drops from the night watch.
The news spread through the city. Yuan Zhu drifted leisurely in a painted boat, while Yu Lou engaged in poetic discourse upon a *huchuang* (a folding chair).

In the ninth month, the reflection of a rainbow encroached upon the steps, and the moonlight fell across the door. It was precisely the season when young women prepare their garments, and the farmers build their garden plots.

At this time, the sound of falling leaves and the warbling of crickets resound; beneath the fences, chrysanthemums newly burst forth in splendor, while ahead on the cliffs, cassia seeds have already begun to waft their fragrance.
Withered red smartweeds cast low shadows as a lone sail returns to the distant bay; withered green paulownias fall in disarray as a single wild goose descends upon the level sands.
Fortunate to encounter such an auspicious season, we reverently perform these Buddhist rites.

Furthermore, as the sun’s charioteer dwells in the lunar mansion of Fang (Mūla) and the Dipper’s handle points toward Xu (Jie), speckled white arums fly along the banks of Chu, and fresh yellow chrysanthemums bloom at the fence of Tao.
The evening fishing songs resound with a single cry of "Kuai-nai" as they return to distant coves; startled by the cold, the ranks of wild geese soar on and on.
Gazing across the vast expanse of the sky, the waters stretch for ten thousand acres as the rice and grain ripen in abundance; frost matures the groves, rich with oranges and tangerines.

On the Double Ninth, clouds drift over the southern marshes, and after the rain clears, the West Mountain reveals itself. The evening cicadas chirp with a piercing, mournful cry, their lamentations echoing through the verdant canopies, startling the observer.
Rows of wild geese soar aloft, their silhouettes casting distant reflections upon the scrolls of sunset clouds. Elegant songs celebrate the "Bestowing of Garments" in the state of Bin;
gatherings coincide with the falling of hats on Mount Longshan. Yuanming (Tao Qian) gathers the golden-hued chrysanthemums; Zhangfang carries jeweled dogwood in his satchel.
Beside the Fengle Tower, the autumn waters stretch far to join the Milky Way; by the side of the Tengwang Pavilion, the cold pond is as crystal clear as a vessel of ice.
As this auspicious season approaches, it is fitting to establish a worthy cause.
In the tenth month, frosty pears offer their fruit and snowy rice steams with fragrance; the green tangerines and yellow oranges monopolize the fine scenery of the year. The chrysanthemums—
The withered lotuses hasten the onset of the cold majesty of the tenth month; evening winds blow over the waters as wild geese form slanting rows.
Night rain drips upon the steps as the cricket’s melody grows piercing. As the beginning of the Great Cold season commences, it is fitting that the Dharma assembly be proclaimed.
Furthermore, the records of the Qin history are upright; Xuanming keeps time to the rhythm. Cold smoke drifts vast and dim as the well-trees shed their leaves in disarray upon the silver bedstead.

Twilight rain falls pitter-patter as the chrysanthemums by the fence wither and scatter against the jade steps. Ten thousand miles away, the heavens are low and the clouds are dark; at this single moment—

The wind is swift and the frost is severe; the sound of crickets mingles with the lengthening watches of the night. The shadows of wild geese follow the pale outlines of the mountains as they grow faint.

Beneath the lower element (the winter solstice), the chrysanthemums on the fence have shed their gold, and ice forms like jade upon the pond. As the season of "Little Spring" arrives, it coincides precisely with the middle of this auspicious month.

In Wujiang, scattered leaves flutter like crows; along the Chu banks, withered reeds hide geese for their night’s rest. Wind-stirred curtains sway like *fei-cui* birds; frost-covered tiles freeze the *yuan-yang* ducks.
At twilight, the sky lowers as faint clouds enshroud the moon’s radiance; the night deepens and waters grow cold, where the severe chill of hoarfrost solemnizes the ripples of the waves.
Wood-apples are split open by the frost of Dongting Lake; oranges are offered as gifts, becoming snow within silver jars.
The first day of the eleventh month has just arrived; one should honor the highest goodness.
The harsh winds of November pierce the curtains, and the short days pass through the drapes. A few rows of guest geese cry out in the vast sky, and a swarm of cold fish huddles together.
The water plants are dense; amidst the bamboo fences and thatched cottages, fragrant plum blossoms secretly spread their scent.
In the rain-swept ravines and frost-covered forests, the gnarled pine branches still stand out in emerald green. As the first yang has returned, all virtues should be honored.

Furthermore, as the Pleiades (Mao) constellation marks the midpoint of midwinter, it is called the "Subsequent Year. The cold wind bites with piercing intensity, arraying the frost upon the *yuanyuan* roof tiles;
dense sleet falls, hastening the urgent snow of the *Tuyuan*. The beasts on the small pavilion are surrounded by the glow of warmth, while within the secluded window—
The plum blossoms drift with fragrance; the deep green of the sturdy bamboos remains as it was. The lush solitude of the lone pine does not change its azure hue.

At the winter solstice, the first yang returns, and the warm musical laws begin. As the six tubes move and the flying ashes shift, the musical pitch turns to Huangzhong, recorded in the *Lushi* as the "Cloud-Book" (Shuyun).
Section. Shadows lengthen as the Han court celebrates the rites of the Xingqing Palace; swift snow dances amidst returning winds, and frozen clouds enshroud the cherished sun.
The waters grow cold at the golden well; ice fills the jade pitcher. The willow’s form already approaches the splendor of the month of La;
the incense powder silently conveys the news of spring. On this auspicious festival, we employ these humble expressions of sincerity.
On the first day of the twelfth month, the north wind blows piercingly, yet the beloved sun shines warmly. River plums burst forth like jade, betraying the arrival of spring;
willow trees along the banks hold gold within their buds, deliberating over the waning year. Cold crows peck for food, circling in groups amidst the sandy islets, while frozen sparrows hide away.
The body shivers beside the eaves of the old house; red animal charcoal blazes within the warm chamber; the light of the fisherman’s lamp reflects upon the cold river.
Fortunate to have encountered the deep winter, one should cultivate the wondrous fruits of merit.

Furthermore, the cold of the twelfth month hastens the willows; the news of spring is delivered by the plum blossoms. In the four fields, clouds hang low, shrouding the fisherman’s boat; they mock the power of wine.
Throughout the heavens, snow dances in wild flight, falling upon the monk’s quarters to dampen the tea-smoke. The *Shi* of Bin records the chanting of ice-drilling; the decree of Lü specifically...
Written on the first day of the month of Chou (the second month).

On the eve of the year’s end, the rain bids farewell to the cold; the north wind escorts in the twelfth month. The piercing frost is so chilling that the thousand households appear as if transformed into jade towers and terraces—a portentous omen.

Snow falls in profusion, transforming ten thousand valleys into a world of silver; the three hundred and sixty days of the year have reached their end, and the seventy-two seasonal signs have come to a close.
The fragrance of pepper blossoms wafts upon golden cups, while the sound of firecrackers fades upon the jade-paved courtyard.
Fortunate to be at this juncture of the New Year’s eve, we reverently perform Buddhist rites to welcome auspiciousness.

When the handle of the Dipper points between two lunar mansions during an intercalary month, one additional month is added; the remaining days take the number that completes the cycle. These accumulated units mirror the odd numbers of the six "fingers" (le) in divination.
This was already proclaimed by the *Zhouguan* in its section on the gate, and specifically recorded in the *Yao Dian* as the completion of the year.
At dawn, the willow eyes conceal mist; the peach cheeks weep dew. As the bells of Xiao Temple wane, the three calls that herald the day urge the journey forward.
When the water-drops at the watchtower cease, a single cry awakens the traveler from his dream. Clouds unroll atop the mountains amidst frequent morning rains; by the desk lies last night’s...
(Morning) The mist dampens the morning robe.
(Spring) The rooster’s cry has just sounded; the butterfly’s dream has just begun to return. Faint stars still linger atop the willow tips;
thick dew has already settled upon the lotus leaves. (Summer)
The shadow of the golden crow appears; the light of the silver river arises. A misty white dew blankets the autumn river;
a rustling clear wind rises at the dawn bank.
(Autumn) The water-clock has ceased its chime; the painted drum’s sound has faded. A hazy morning light reflects across the level fields; the faint morning glow floats upon the horizon.
Distant peaks; the wooden bridge is slippery with frost, the river road is severe with wind. Fortunate to face the dawn, we extensively perform Buddhist rites.

(Winter) At noon, the blue sky is at its zenith; the red sun is precisely at midday. The myriad phenomena of mountains and rivers all face the light. The neighboring flocks of chickens cry out in unison.

At noon, the shadows of the courtyard flowers fall in layered and overlapping patterns upon the jade terrace. At the hour of *bhu*, the light flickers through the willows along the embankment, their branches— some short, some long—
enveloping the ornate thoroughfare.

The shade of the locust trees shifts at midday; the shadows of the willows move toward the west. Slanting sunlight plays with lingering crimson through half the window; light smoke drags a pale purple across the nine main thoroughfares.
Herds of sheep press together as they return along perilous paths; swarms of bees gather in confusion, their buzzing heralding the start of their official session.
In the evening, the sun’s orb is about to fall; the hare-marked moon is about to rise. The setting sun, clutching the mountain peaks, is half-present and half-absent;
the lingering sunset reflected on the water flickers between light and extinction. Travelers rushing their journey are as frantic as arrows; old fishermen rowing their boats are as swift as shuttles.
Furthermore, returning crows hold the wild colors of the fields; sleeping geese stir the autumnal sounds. The golden crow (the sun) is about to fall behind the western mountains;

the jade hare (the moon) feels ashamed to rise from the eastern sea. Within a path of white clouds, a cowherd passes through a rustic gate blowing his flute; at the head of a rapid water rapids, a fisherman...
The old man rows his boat back to the willow-lined bank;
at night, the jade towers stir once more. The Milky Way shines with starlight, while flickering phoenix candles sway in the breeze and the fishermen’s lamps dot the scene like scattered jewels.
Reflecting in the water, fireflies illuminate the face of the green grass; the moonlight pierces through the head of the azure clouds.

At midnight, the hour of Zi arrives; the Yin is at its height and Yang begins to arise. The moonlight is now at its zenith; the clarity of day resembles water as the tally-sticks of the night clock pass one after another.
The night deepens; the candle flames flicker repeatedly as we approach the third watch. Through the forest bamboo, golden light filters through; in the courtyard flowers, jade-like radiance plays.
Ten thousand *li* away, the wind is clear and the mists roll back; across the heavens, the Dipper turns and the stars shift.

On a moonlit night, a clear breeze enters the seat; the bright moon ascends into the void. Flower shadows cover the ground in jade-like brilliance; bamboo shadows invade the steps in golden fragments.

A clear sun adorns the mountains and rivers; the wind stirs through the fields and lanes. Several scrolls of fine silk display radiant colors; a thousand layers of brocade cluster with fresh patterns.
Flowers and grasses waft their fragrance; birds and fish find their delight.
The rain-clouds drive forth iron cavalry; lightning flashes like golden serpents. Heaven-shaking peals of thunder resound, and torrents of rain pour down as if overturning the ocean.
The Shang-yang bird dances forth; the stone swallows fly aloft. Thick clouds densely shroud the peaks of Mount Jiu- Yi; a fine rain secretly adds to the three-tiered waves.
The rain clears.
The Yuelu Peak gathers the clouds; heaven and earth clear after the rain. The green mountains remain unchanged through the ages, their ancient trees casting dense, dark shadows;
the blue waves have newly increased, as ten-thousand acres of vast surges roll on and on.
Snow freezes as clouds hang like curtains; fine snow flies like jade. The sorrowful sparrows on the eaves are silent; the cold fish dwelling among the algae do not feed.
The blossoming plum cannot be distinguished; the rising gulls leave no trace. Fragments of broken jade fall profusely upon the fisherman’s cloak; they fall densely and in disarray.
A silver-hued fluttering crane-feather cloak.
When the snow clears, the vast sky is bright with falling flakes; a pale moon enshrouds the sands. Cold presses down upon the *sùxiāng* quilt; frost penetrates the *qǐquè* palace. A brilliant hue—
The plum blossoms add richness in the shadows; the green shoots clearly announce the safety of the bamboo.
The water-lands and river-cities transform into a world of three thousand silver realms; the pavilions and wine terraces become twelve jade towers.
Frost and dew congeal at Kunming Lake; the waves grow cold at Taiye Pond. Flying-Lien roars and bellows, and the vegetation across the thousand districts withers away.
The majesty of Qingnü brings desolation to the gardens and groves of the four fields. It is the season when leaves fall to return to their roots, and flowers begin to bud.
Regarding the occasion of seeing the Buddha:

on the day of Śākyamuni’s birth (the eighth day of the fourth month), the morning was moistened by the plum rains, and the midday was refreshed by the fragrance of the catalpa breeze. The eight-leafed *míng* plant grew upon the steps of Yao, and the five-stringed lute was played.
In the corridors of Yu, tall willows hush with the new cicadas; in the magnificent halls, nursing swallows fly about.

It is precisely the season of pure harmony under the reign of Yan Di, and the very time of the Tathāgata’s birth. Auspicious light shines brilliantly, permeating the Zen groves; auspicious mists gather luxuriantly, enshrouding the Buddhist temples.
With sincere devotion, we specially perform this rite of celebration.
On the birthday of Amitābha (the seventeenth day of the eleventh month), the summer calendar is renewed;
it is the first month of the returning Yang, when the *míng* leaves on Emperor Yao’s steps have just reached their second sprout.
The human world has its snow transformed into jade towers; beyond the passes, the plum blossoms perfume the realm.
This is the season of the North Emperor’s rigorous cold, coinciding with the auspicious occasion of Amitābha’s birthday.
On the nineteenth day of the second month, the birthday of Avalokiteśvara, four leaves of the *míng* tree have fallen.
It is the middle month of spring; at ten thousand households, the curtains are rolled up as fragrant breezes blow, and across ten thousand miles of rivers and mountains, auspicious radiance floats.
Purple swallows seek their nests, dancing in pairs upon the carved beams; yellow orioles call for companions, flying side by side in twos.
Transplanted upon lofty trees, the official willows manifest the color of True Suchness (*tathatā*); the immortal flowers emit the fragrance of precept and meditative concentration (*śīla-samādhi*).
They spread the radiant light of the Azure Emperor and adorn the birthday festival of Avalokiteśvara.

On the birthday of the Sage Emperor (the twenty-eighth day of the third month), the willows by the embankment hang their filaments, yet they cannot bind the magnificent scenery of the three months of spring; the flowers in the courtyard cluster like brocade, still retaining the lingering fragrance for two more days.
The Lord of the East hastens the auspicious season; the Sage Emperor has fortunately encountered this birth festival.

On the birthday of Huaguang (the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month), the cassia fruits bloom in splendor, coinciding with the fullness of autumn. Though the chrysanthemums are late to bloom, they still retain their fragrance for two more days.

When Wuyuan was pregnant with its excellence, it was precisely the time when the waters of He stored their brilliance. Auspicious signs unfolded from a single tree, and a divine omen responded with the Five Kings.
Fortunate indeed that we encounter the arrival of this birth festival; it is fitting that we exhaust our sincere hearts in offering congratulations.
The Recorded Sayings of Master Yin of Gaofeng Longquan Monastery, Volume One;
The Recorded Sayings of Master Yin of Gaofeng Longquan Monastery, Volume Two.
Compiled by the junior disciple Ruying, Abbot of Liuzu Monastery.
Petition for the Ritual of Empowerment for the Buddha-Service of Entering the Mandala:
I reverently hear that the Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space; manifesting forms in response to beings, it is like the moon reflected in water. As I reflect upon this...
I, the monk [Name], am fortunate to dwell in the Central Kingdom and have the honor of being a son of Śākyamuni.

I am indebted for the virtue of Heaven and Earth’s encompassing embrace and moved by the grace of the Sovereign and Teacher’s bestowed instructions. In spirit, I have awakened to the vehicle of the Dharma, and in heart, I am without retreat.

On this auspicious occasion, may the legacy of Ānanda from days of yore be shared equally by monastics and laity alike; and may the faithful lay devotees, honoring these roots of merit, find benefit for both the living and the deceased. Thus it is said:
The assembly of the netherworld and the living world is convened, and the Water and Land feast is opened. I, the monk [Name], though dull by nature, am not lacking in clarity of mind.

Adhering to the teachings of the World-Honored One at Vulture Peak and following the ritual protocols of the Tiantai Master Zhiyi, I fear that in proclaiming these matters I may lack order and propriety, and in offering praises and prayers I may be negligent or erroneous.
I hereby present my sincerity in advance, daring to intrude upon Your Enlightened Awareness.

Your Majesty, we humbly pray that you will compassionately extend your protection and grace. May it be so that our minds may uphold the Dharma-seal, preserving within the subtle spontaneity of nature;

and that our mouths may recite the true teachings, reaching the sacred hearing of Your Majesty without deviation. Now that this Dharma assembly has been inaugurated, we hope for Your Majesty’s guardianship so that this sublime gathering may reach its full completion.
We respectfully offer this confession and thanksgiving. We, the monk [Name], are truly prostrate with awe and trepidation.
With the utmost urgency and trepidation, I have composed this text for the purification of the three karmas.
As the Milky Way shines brightly and the jade-dripping clock deepens its resonance, the heavens shift as the constellations turn; across ten thousand *li*, [the night deepens].
The wind was clear and the mist rolled away. At first, the Dharma music of Mount Yushan was performed; then, the bright incense of *kṣīra-śarkarā* (chicken-tongue) was ignited.

Beating the Dharma drum and blowing the Dharma conch, the sound reached far and near; prostrating before the Brahma-like countenance and chanting Brahma-songs, they welcomed and gathered the holy sages.
Fruits clustered upon golden platters, as if Śrīgupta had gathered them; flowers arranged in precious vessels, as if Bhadrapāla had brought them.
A single good deed once arisen, ten thousand transgressions are all cleansed. The defilements of body and mind are purified by relying on the water of the Dharma;
the karma of anger and resentment is eliminated by depending on the wind of compassion. This ensures that the physical body is pure and allows the Dharma-body to be perfectly luminous.
Their moral conduct is lofty and solitary; their wisdom-mind is never obscured. Lay devotees extend their earnest prayers; the monastic community maintains solemn and reverent decorum.
With single-minded devotion and respectful gravity, each purifies the three karmas. Now, please recite the Mantra for Purifying the Three Karmas.
Furthermore,

as the dripping water from the bronze pitcher marks the shifting of the stars across the Milky Way, precisely at the moment when the celestial music first fades away and the weariness of worldly toil momentarily ceases,
the golden incense burner burns fragrance that pervades all realms, and the jade chimes strike a melody that mutes the clouds, amidst clusters of flowers.
Clustered like brocade, the lamps blaze and the candles shine. High-lifted is the upward-pointing vehicle of the ancestral lineage; grandly performed are the boundless Buddha-activities.
One must cause the karma of body, speech, and mind to be pure, and ensure that the faculties of precept, concentration, and wisdom are perfected and luminous.
The teachings contain mantras, which you should recite as before. Furthermore,

since the site of practice (maṇḍala) is pure as ice and the minds of the assembly are as focused as sunflowers turning toward the sun, one should burn the incense of precepts, the incense of concentration, the incense of wisdom, and the incense of liberation.

Incense; the ritual sprinkling of water for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and the Mahā-yan-water. Flowers cluster like brocade in the three springs; lamps burn like stars across the One Han.
When the jade chimes ring, they vibrate with a grand, resonant sound; where the golden gongs resound, they harmonize with the *bherī* drum in a shimmering cadence.
The wind of the Way opens the flowers of the *utpala*; the rain of virtue nourishes the grasses of the *bhikṣu*. The six sense objects...
Internally pure, the nature of consciousness is perfectly luminous; the five turbidities externally dispelled, the Dharma-body is pristine.
May you deign to examine this single-minded, humble petition; we shall maintain the mantras of the three karmas (as before).
Furthermore, consider that phenomena arise from the mind, and the mind transforms according to phenomena.

If one can achieve purity in a single thought-moment, then the ten directions will become serene, like the bright moon suspended in the sky, resembling a lotus flower emerging from the water. The nature of bodhi-wisdom is fundamentally...
Perfectly luminous, yet afflictions and adventitious dust give rise to deluded discrimination. One forcibly drives away the monkey that craves water and stones;
lost in wandering, one picks up flower-needles. The turning of light resides entirely within the person; purity must rely upon the secret mantra (as before).
Furthermore, golden ducks waft fragrant incense as auspicious vapors rise; jade-insect lamps spread forth brilliant and auspicious light.
Desiring to purify the six sense-objects, one should cleanse the three karmas (as before).

Having purified the three karmas through the application of fragrant ointment and the rinsing of the palms, all internal and external defilements are eliminated; one’s essence becomes identical to that of all Tathāgatas, and both body and mind are entirely pure.
Next, using fragrant ointment and pure water, recite the *Gandhahastaka-dhāraṇī* in verse (*gāthā*): [Insert dhāraṇī here]
As soon as a single drop of scented ointment is applied, the defilements of the six sense objects are entirely eliminated.
Next, one should take refuge in the Bhagavān; may his compassion grant protection. (Recite the mantra.)
Prayer for Incense:
It is considered that while the Dharmakāya is unmoving, all who have a sincere resonance with it find their needs met; the Sage’s eye is not distant, so there is no prayer that is not answered.
To convey the faith of the ten directions, one must transmit the incense of the five divisions. This incense is the seed of the roots of merit.
Cultivated within the ground of the mind, its purity and uniqueness are inherently natural; how could its carving and shaping be the work of human effort?
It ranks first among the clusters of orchids and musk; it holds supremacy peerless within the groves of sandalwood. When burned, auspicious vapors rise from the golden incense burner;
as it disperses, auspicious clouds drift across the jade palace. As soon as a single wisp of cold smoke arises, the Buddhas of the ten directions hear it from afar. Its fragrance permeates all.

Having perfected the incense of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, it is universally offered to the upper, middle, and lower realms. Desiring to transmit these sublime verses, I humbly rely upon this profound resonance:
the incense of precepts, the incense of concentration, the incense of wisdom, the incense of liberation, and the incense of the knowledge and vision of liberation.

With clouds of radiant light pervading the entire Dharma-realm, I make offerings to the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions; I make offerings to the most profound and subtle Dharma; I make offerings to the Arhats of the four fruits.

The Chinese monk makes offerings to the assembly of all holy sages; through seeing and hearing, they are universally perfumed by the bliss of the true and eternal. So it is for the humans and devas of the Dharma-realm as well.
Incense is offered as an oblation to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. Disciple now offers this incense to all sentient beings.
It was likewise so. He constantly aspired to remain before the Buddha.
Furthermore, when the site of enlightenment first opened, the fragrant chamber arose first; surging auspicious vapors formed its dais, and billowing clouds of felicity served as its canopy.
I pay homage to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. May this reach the ears of the myriad spirits of heaven, earth, and the waters.
If one wishes to express even a fraction of sincere devotion, one should first burn incense of a hundred-fold fragrance (as previously described).
Furthermore, these are fragrances: the *campaka* is renowned for its excellence, and *candana* is prized for its high value. As they are burned in golden censers, auspicious smoke billows forth;

as it permeates the celestial vault, auspicious vapors swirl in profusion. Reaching everywhere before the Triple Gem throughout the ten directions, it extends far to the four palaces and the myriad...
Above the spiritual, it penetrates the utmost sincerity of the ordinary mind; it serves as the wondrous gateway for all manner of goodness.

Furthermore, this incense possesses a rare and extraordinary nature with pure roots and trunk. It is sometimes called by the name "chicken-tongue" (keshé), and sometimes designated as "ox-head" (niúhóu).

With this title as its head, one may convey sincerity to the Spirit Mountain and communicate with the truth of the Ocean Treasury; perfuming oneself with the fragrance of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, one universally offers these to the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.

Wherever the Sanskrit sounds of this *An-shui-wen* (Text of Consolation) first arise, and whenever the music of the Dharma first resounds, the golden resonance shakes the mountains and rivers, while the jade verses secretly stir heaven and earth.
I am deeply concerned that in various regions there may be prohibitions against this place; how could the dragon deities not feel a sense of awe and trepidation?
I shall rely upon the power of consolation. Within the scriptural treasury (piṭaka) of our Buddha, the Tathāgata, there exists the Mantra for Consoling the Local Deities (Kṣetrapāla).
I shall now reverently recite it. [Gāthā:]

The various numinous spirits of the mountains, rivers, peaks, and marshes, and the many dragon deities of this local territory—upon hearing the sublime mantra proclaimed, each dwells in its respective quarter and gives rise to joy. (Recite the mantra.)
Furthermore, I reverently hear that your majestic golden countenance and radiant white *ūrṇā* hairs reveal you as the Teacher of the Three Realms and the Father of the four classes of beings.
In your conduct, the Brahma King leads the way before you; in your movements, Śakra follows behind. Bodhisattvas surround you, and the Asuras [attend at your side].

Regarding external protection: ten thousand billion banners and streamers flash and shimmer; hundreds of thousands of gongs and drums resound with clamor. Winds and clouds are shattered and dispersed; rivers and seas boil and surge.
The *gandharva*s’ helmets emit flames, and the spears and halberds of the *yakṣa* hosts produce a chilling cold. Upon merely reaching the gateway, there is fear that one might violate taboos.
Our Buddha, the Tathāgata, has taught a True Mantra for comforting the local deities (*bhūmidevatā*); I shall now reverently recite it.
(As before). The ritual assembly for purifying the waters has been inaugurated with radiant splendor.
With sincere and profound devotion, one desires to welcome the various sages to descend; this must necessarily rely upon the [offerings from] the four quarters.
To purify [the site], we rely upon the water of the Dharma to sprinkle the *maṇḍala*. As for this water: Kunlun conceives its excellence, and the Milky Way flows its fragrance.
Within the scent of lotus flowers, the azure waves are cold; from the tips of willow branches, sweet dew is sprinkled.

The three mountains of Mount Penglai face one another in mutual respect, and a single stream of Caoxi flows on forever. It stirs auspicious winds so that the jade ripples across a thousand rivers, and turns forth sudden rains.

The silver ladle pushes forth the four great rivers; when spring warmth reaches the Dragon Gate, the fish leap through its three tiers. When the autumn wind rises over the vast sea, the Peng bird soars ten thousand miles.
Within the pool of seven jewels, jade characters are inscribed; from the mouths of the nine dragons, the Golden Immortals bathe.

All living beings rely on this to moisten their parched and withered forms; the great earth depends on it to eliminate all defilement. Relying upon the Buddha’s water, may it be sprinkled universally upon this Dharma assembly to wash away the myriad impurities.
May the darkness and confusion of the kalpas forever attain the purity of the Single Truth. Gāthā:

The nectar-water from the Bodhisattva’s willow branch can cause a single drop to sprinkle throughout the ten directions, completely eliminating all foul odors, impurities, and defilements, so that this site of practice (bodhimaṇḍa) is entirely purified. Recite the mantra.
Furthermore, as for water: its numinous currents originate from on high; who can fathom its wondrous source? When the moon shines bright over the four seas, it is profound and limpid, pure as jade;
when the winds are stilled at the Nine Rivers, it flows vast and wide, as brilliant as falling frost and sparkling snow. It nourishes the small; it nourishes the great.
Great! There is nothing to which it is unsuited. Whether one directs it east or west, there is no direction that is not beneficial.
Caoqi’s ancient tradition transmits a single drop; Yaoshan once pointed toward the four quarters. Shangshan extolled its illustrious reputation, and Liangrou preserved its true nature.

When one tastes this drop, one’s very bones and hair become light and refreshing, thereby removing the dust and vexations of the outflows (*āsrava*). To drink it is to purify the heart and gallbladder.

Cooling! It can extinguish boundless heat and affliction. Therefore, from within the emerald lapis lazuli flask of the King of Ambrosia, upon the green willow branch of Avalokiteśvara, it is sprinkled drop by drop without partiality; wherever it touches, there is constant moisture.
Relying upon this Buddha-water, may the entire Dharma assembly be universally purified (as before).

Furthermore, it is water. It becomes square or round according to its vessel; it fills or empties as circumstances dictate. It melts in spring and freezes in winter; it flows in the trigram Kan and rests in Gen.
Vast indeed is its wondrous source, unfathomable; surging indeed is its spiritual current, inexhaustible. Green ravines hide dragons; cold ponds soak [the earth].
The Moon: sometimes it transforms into waves of grace beneath the dragon-brush of a sovereign; sometimes it dwells upon the willow branch of a Bodhisattva, sprinkling nectar.
As soon as a single drop flies forth, the ten directions are all purified (as before).
To eliminate impurities, one must examine the utility of things; yet their natures are often muddled. When water fulfills its Way, its mind is profoundly deep and still.
If one cultivates the six repositories [of the body], one fully realizes what is appropriate for nourishment. If one aligns them with the five elements, one exhausts the beauty of what they moisten.
When stirred, it gives rise to light breezes and waves; when still, the bright moon shines with crystalline clarity.

We look up to the Tathāgata for his wondrous power of creation and take refuge in the sustaining force of the empowerment of Krodhavajra. This virtuous water is transformed into various pure substances for ritual application.
Heaven does not withhold its Way, descending as an auspicious sign of sweet nectar; Earth does not withhold its treasures, surging forth as a portentous omen of the spring of ambrosia.
There is not a single thing that does not receive the benefit of this moistening grace, causing the ten directions to become entirely pure sites for the Way.
There is a verse in the teachings that removes all defilement:
Furthermore, earth, water, fire, and wind combine with yin and yang to stand together; putridity, stench, filth, and defilement mingle with the ordinary and the holy to dwell side by side.
Afflictions and anxieties are profound, and the karma of love and hatred is heavy; one is constantly oppressed by the four serpents and further assailed by two mice.

The five hindrances have not yet been eliminated, and the eight impurities are difficult to remove; therefore, one relies on the water of the Dharma to wash away all darkness and delusion, and secretly draws upon the power of mantras to cleanse all manner of defilements and turbidity.

Universally transformed by the mingling of incense clouds billowing like dense mists and flower rains falling in profusion, the sound of Brahma-voices resounds through the nine heavens and the music of the Dharma vibrates throughout the ten stages.
Banners and multicolored streamers are evenly distributed across the three islands, while the light of smoke, mist, lamps, and candles intermingles as it descends from above.

One day, as the stars and constellations were arrayed in the six harmonies, the Three Virtues proclaimed their teachings. The kitchen of Xiangji was grandly opened, and the fruits of the Immortal Source were universally offered.
Golden words were loftily expounded, and jade scrolls were frequently proclaimed. Adornments were arrayed before the Zimo Buddha, and offerings were spread beside the emerald lotus pedestal.
Invitations were extended to thousands of worthies and ten thousand sages; they took refuge in the Five Eyes and Six Supernatural Powers, gazing toward the Dharma.
May Your Majesty deign to grace us with Your presence, descending from Your fragrant chariot. We fear that the offerings we have prepared may be insufficient to reach every part;
we therefore rely upon mantras to ensure they are made complete and abundant. Gāthā:
The Buddha bestowed the ambrosial water of *agada*; the Sangha maintains inconceivable transformations. A single treasure and a single meal are immeasurable in extent;
ten thousand sages and a thousand worthies are all fully satisfied. Recite the mantra.
A Text in Praise of the Triple Gem:
I reverently contemplate the Buddha Jewel. Having accumulated vast causes, he has perfected the marks of the full moon.
His merit is supreme and beyond limit; his practice is profound and inexhaustible. Sublime indeed is the Tathāgata Kanakamuni; how great is Vairocana!

The Patriarch: His brilliance was all-pervasive as he manifested his own efficacy; his solitary practice was most authentic. His Way was unfathomable, yet the more it was measured, the deeper it became;
his merit was impossible to transmit, yet its transmission grew ever more distant. Unborn and undying, he sat loftily, severing all ties within the city of Nirvana;

without past or present, he dwelt in profound stillness, never departing from the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī). Upon the Vajra Throne, he expounded the Dharma-truths of the Three Vehicles. He opened...
With the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence in the Deer Park, he subdued the heretics of Pāpīyān, causing them to kneel and accept his victory;

he drove away fierce tigers and venomous dragons, causing them to humble their majesty and submit in docility. When the sun and moon arise, they shine brilliantly like the light from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
The Yangtze and Han rivers wash his vastness, which is like the ocean of the Dharma within his breast. Unstained by mud and unthinned by grinding, his virtue will equal the Great Void.
Unburned by fire and unwetted by water, his conduct will be as firm as gold and jade.
Abiding in the wondrous existence yet not clinging to it, dwelling in non-action yet not ceasing to act, even when gods and dragons pay him homage, he never relaxes his countenance; [even] Śakra...

How could one ever turn away from him whom we revere and honor? His countenance is majestic and exceedingly subtle; he is titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans. His grace permeates the boundless reaches, and his transformation is bestowed without a presiding agent.
When he preaches the Dharma, the words are near at hand yet the purport is profound; when he inaugurates the teaching, the source is deep and the current is long.
He manifests distinct names as the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*, and different temporal reckonings as the great eons (*mahākalpa*) and small eons (*antarakalpa*). Thus he appears...
Your supernormal powers reach as high as seven *tāla* trees; your manifestation of wondrous marks surpasses even Sumeru, the King of Mountains.

Is this not indeed so? Is it not true and beyond doubt? We humbly pray that you will for a time leave the moon-palaces by the waterside and slowly mount your wind-horses and cloud-chariots, with banners and streamers shining in five-colored splendor, and celestial music resounding in eight tones with piercing clarity. May you emit the jade-like light from between your brows to illuminate all living beings.
Sprinkling nectar to moisten the parched and withered; since there is resonance that permeates all, what could one seek that would not be answered?
We look up to Your Sacred Majesty to deign to descend upon this site of practice.
As for the Dharma Jewel: it is the bequeathed word of the Great Awakened One, the Dharma-joy for all living beings, containing most profound and abstruse meanings and secret, mysterious texts.

The Dragon Kings revered it and stored it within the oceanic treasury; Śakra, the Lord of Devas, honored it and held it aloft with celestial hands. King Aśoka personally transcribed it, drawing his blood as a brush for the Tripiṭaka;
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty attained sudden enlightenment through single-minded sincerity, ordaining monks and constructing temples. To speak of its far-reaching influence...
Thus, there is Prime Minister Pei Xiu’s exposition on the meaning of the *Awakening of Faith*, and Bai Juyi’s preface to the *Sutra of the Radiant Light*.
To speak of those more recent, there is Wang Shu-wang’s translation of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and Zhang Wujin’s commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
How magnificent are the over five thousand scrolls of the *Bai-ye* (palmyra) manuscripts! How vast and expansive are the twelve divisions of the Sanskrit scriptures!
Thus it is. Those who recite it are like a blind person whose cataracts are cleared away, suddenly beholding blue and yellow;
those who realize its meaning are like the heavens when the clouds have parted, clearly seeing the stars and constellations.

Since the translation relied upon the Great Being Kumārajīva and the manifestation of its spiritual power depended upon the Venerable Master Dharmaruci, spanning from antiquity to the present day and encompassing heaven and earth, the events remain hidden though contemplated, and the words remain obscure though they exist.
It serves as the provisional gateway for all birth and death, and acts as an imperishable classic and essential guide for ten thousand generations.
On the assembly at Vulture Peak in days of yore, one heard only of the entrustment to Kāśyapa; how could it have been transmitted to Shenxiu at the head of Mount Dayu at that time?
Those kings and sovereigns who reverently upheld it caused their great schemes to consolidate both heaven and earth. One must truly accept and believe this.
Those who uphold this practice will find that their lands and people attain great prosperity and their descendants flourish.

This can serve as a gracious torch for those in the three miserable realms and as a ladder and vessel for those in the six paths of existence. Those who merely flatter with their words are like those who hold a torch to burn the sky, only to find themselves exhausted and defeated.
Those who add redundant and superfluous explanations are like those who shoot arrows at the sky, achieving nothing but drawing blood upon their own arms.
Profound! What is called the exhaustion of the refined and the subtle, neither increasing nor decreasing—only when such is present is the work accomplished.

I humbly pray that the majestic elephant carriage, towering and magnificent, shall carry it afar from the Flower Treasury Sea; that the Dragon Kings, leaping for joy, shall swiftly support it forth from the Crystal Palace.
The jade casket opens and the sandalwood rollers ring out with resonance; the precious cloth unfurls and the luster of the ink blazes forth. May it turn [back]...
The phoenixes dance with joy; the magpies shed their disheveled plumage. It is like the Milky Way forming a celestial pattern, as if one were beholding a grand vision from above.
May it be that by opening the hands and casting the eyes upon this, one may cast away delusive thoughts and reach the True Source;

and by contemplating with the mind and upholding it in the heart, one may accord with the Original Ground and awaken to the Absolute Truth. With a deeply stirred heart, unable to remain at ease, I prostrate myself in refuge and reverently pray.
As for the Jewel of the Sangha: they cultivate wisdom through the mind and awaken to the fundamental principle through the nature of reality.
Desiring to transcend the ten stages (*bhūmi*), they first study the ten categories; desiring to penetrate the three barriers, they first clarify the three karmas.

Unfettered by worldly conditions and severed from all attachments, they remain perfectly beyond the dust and defilements such that nothing can disturb them. Floating like an unmoored boat, the Way will transform them spontaneously. Radiant...

He is luminous yet does not dazzle; he is trustworthy yet does not deceive. Having long dwelt within the groves of knowledge and wisdom, he has profoundly entered the threshold of the Patriarchs' domain.
Day by day and month by month he advances, practicing his cultivation as if treading upon thin ice, and progressing toward the Way as if beginning to build a mountain with the first basket of earth.
He waters the flowers and draws the water, plucking leaves and tracing branches; his body is like a drifting cloud emerging from a mountain peak.
One may know his sovereign mastery; his will is like that of a great eagle soaring in the heavens, for only then can one believe in his solitary loftiness.

Alas! Below, he awakens to the profound mechanism; holding the head, he clarifies the essential purport. He possesses the spirit of a shout that scatters white clouds; he possesses the tongs and hammer that shatter empty space.
In rolling up and unfolding, he establishes heaven and earth beyond the square; in extending and crossing, he hangs the sun and moon within the realm. By means of softness and humility...

He took the emptiness of the aggregates as his banner and the profound stillness as his primary tenet. Continuing the flame and linking the fragrance, he transmitted the robe and succeeded to the patriarchs.
Of ten questions, he answered nine with silence; the Way was present in the very act of looking. A single shout left him deaf for three days; the words remained ringing in his ears.
He cultivated himself alone, taking nothing from others; he loved others before ever seeking it for himself. He boarded the vessel of Prajñā to roam the waters of Lake Anavatapta.

In the midst [of it], he rested beneath a coral tree, leaning upon a staff carved from a rabbit’s horn. His eyebrows hung down a span; as he sat amidst the snow, he perceived only the autumn of the waterfall pool.
With his patched robe covering half his shoulder, where the clouds moved, he gradually distanced himself from the dusty world.

Right and wrong were both extinguished; fame and profit were equally forgotten. Whether silent or speaking, his nature was naturally luminous; neither existent nor non-existent, his mind was naturally firm. Truly...
How marvelous this is! Is it not truly so? I prostrate myself and pray that you will unroll your cloud-like robes, mount your jade qilin, and briefly leave your meditation seat;
loosen the straps of your bag and bowl, take up your khakkhara staff, and descend slightly from your rope-corded couch. May you follow these steps while scattering fragrant flowers.
You who roam at will amidst the wind and moon; you who tread upon the five peaks and carry the jade bowl across the sea; you who fly through the air with the six-ringed golden staff.
We pray that you descend upon this Sahā world to bear witness. Do not remain at the top of the hundred-foot pole, but please advance further.
I now prostrate myself and respectfully await your arrival; the faithful layman bows deeply and reverently invites you.

Furthermore, the faithful were solemn and reverent, and the monastics’ minds were focused and single-minded. The melodies of the *Laṅkāvatāra* resounded through the Three Heavens, and the sound of the *Prajñāpāramitā* reached the Ten Stages.
The Great Hero’s descent into the world was like the moon appearing in a clear pool; the Sage’s power in rousing compassion was like a voice transmitted across the distance.

The Empty Valley. Compassionate Father of the four modes of birth, King of Physicians for the three realms, worthy of offerings in heavens and among men, bringing benefit and salvation to other lands and this world.
Performing rare Buddha-works from antiquity to the present, he expounds the supreme Dharma-gate, transcending the mundane and entering the sacred.
Seated upright upon the thousand-petaled lotus throne, he constantly radiates the white jade light of his brow-hair, its sound pervading all.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the golden-hued marks are widely diffused; a thousand billion bodies manifest, responding to all who have faith.
Adorned with the thirty-two marks, they appear without fixed form or limit. That night, the Dharma assembly was inaugurated with solemn and exquisite preparations.
First, the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha was invited to serve as witnesses; next, the myriad spirits of heaven, earth, and water were summoned.

We humbly pray that you will deign to look down upon us with your compassionate gaze. We beseech you to radiate the brilliance of your jade-like brow-hair and manifest the splendor of your golden body.
May hundreds of thousands of holy assemblies attend you and ten billion divine spirits surround you, all descending in due order to this place of practice.
Never forsaking your compassion, may you bear witness to our meritorious virtues.

Praise for the Protectors of the Dharma, who follow the Three Jewels. The Four Kings who protect the Dharma manifest their sacred virtue with dignified majesty; their divine countenances stand forth with extraordinary loftiness.
They wield precious swords that shatter the hearts of demons, and ring golden bells that strike terror into the minds of heretics. Their heroic spirit surges forth in full vigor.
His majestic aura is awe-inspiring. When he moves, his banners and streamers obscure the sun; when he marches, his spears and halberds stand as dense as clouds.

His mere glance causes the Five Peaks to tremble, and his roar of command causes the myriad spirits to prostrate. His divine majesty is manifest yet unfathomable; he protects the Dharma teachings so that they endure forever.
His merit is truly immeasurable, and his virtue is difficult to fully recount. Responding to our present earnest invocation, we pray that you will deign to descend and appear before us.
The Text for the Great Cakra Boundary:
I have heard that the Buddha’s compassion is vast and its praises inexhaustible. As the teachings were transmitted, my heart sought them and responded on this night.
Light incense wafts gently and silver candles shine brightly; yet, fearing that non-Buddhists or celestial māras might create further obstructions, I [proceed].
The fragrance of these lamp-flames has not yet reached us; we must rely upon the majestic radiance of our Buddha to cause the Dharma-seal to be accomplished.

Thus, may the celestial Māras fold their hands in submission and the non-Buddhists turn their hearts toward the Way. May they protect the site of practice and strictly maintain the boundaries of the altar.
Now, the golden bells sway gently and the precious vajra-drum rotates; let us chant the sound of the ocean tide and recite the hymns of Central India.
Mantra. I venture to borrow this pure ground to establish a ritual arena of a hundred jewels. First, I shall summon the Six Heavenly Kings;

next, I will recite the teachings of the five families of Yoga. I pray that the Three Bodies of the Subduer and the Four Wisdoms of the Benevolent One will together deign to descend and bear witness to this consecration of the boundary.
(Recite: Our Original Teacher, Śākya-muni Buddha. (All kneel and ring the bell. The Son of the Śākyas specially proclaims the teachings from his golden mouth;
Relying solely upon the light of the Buddha’s jade-white brow, we entreat him to protect this ritual site with his celestial chariot, By means of these secret mantras and esoteric verses.
Each sound ascends to the realms of devas and immortals; Every phrase opens the gates of hell below.
Should there be any *wangliang* spirits or malevolent demons, They shall be instantly exterminated and compelled to submit to the Right Path.
If one seeks purity throughout the ten directions, One must first invoke and request the six Heavenly Kings.
Hearing that you have arrived to proclaim the secret words, we beseech you to bear witness to our empowerment and seal this sacred boundary.

We reverently burn bright incense and prostrate ourselves in homage. With single-minded devotion, we respectfully invite the thousand-billion emanations of the Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, whose light encompasses all phenomena and whose virtue protects the four classes of beings. May you, in your majesty, descend upon this site of practice. Throughout...
Having successively verified the establishment of the boundary, the lay devotee, with sincere devotion, personally prostrates himself.
He has invited the Heavenly Kings of the Six Directions to descend upon this ritual site to act as the Buddha’s representatives in performing the Dharma rites for this night.
I, the monk [Name], have firmly established the boundaries of the six directions; let no malevolent spirits or demons intrude upon the ritual site, so that the Dharma assembly may proceed.
It stabilizes the radiance. It extols and expounds the Tathāgata’s true discourse. Wherever incense smoke arises constitutes a boundary; wherever lamp light shines constitutes a boundary;
wherever scented water is sprinkled constitutes a boundary; wherever the Brahma-voice penetrates constitutes a boundary; wherever the sound of bells vibrates constitutes a boundary.

Where the gongs and cymbals resound, the boundaries are established: the celestial boundary is bound, the terrestrial boundary is bound, and the boundaries of the cardinal directions are bound; this must rely upon merit.
Having thus completed the circuit, the sages of the three realms are summoned, and the myriad spirits are invoked with clear expectation that they may respond.

Now, according to the ritual teachings and in accordance with the bequeathed instructions, we first present this invocation and subsequently recite the true mantras. We humbly entreat your vast compassion to secretly bestow your protective grace. (Proceeds as follows)
(From the *Ghanṭā*:).
I respectfully invoke the assembly of siddhis as numerous as the sands of the Ganges— the Dharma-body noble ones,
the Great Wheel-King, the maṇḍalas of the five families of yoga, with the Consecrated Vajra as their foremost.
A single body manifests one hundred and eight arms; each hand forms a *dhāraṇī* mudrā, emitting surging flames and the roar of thunderbolts.
Subduing demons, malevolent spirits, and all non-Buddhists, they leap and dance through the air, brandishing wheels, swords, and blades, while their mouths roar like the crashing of thunder.
Rolling his eyes and casting glances like flashes of lightning, his wrathful furrowed brow is truly fearsome.
Possessing great supernatural powers and sovereign mastery, he hears everything from afar as soon as it is uttered;
his coming and going occurs in a single kṣaṇa. The majestic and heroic power of this Noble One is unfathomable.
Holding a golden lasso and a *vajra* for subduing demons, with feet treading upon jewels to pacify Jambudvīpa, the Youth scatters celestial flowers from his four faces.
Come to bind the boundary of the Samādhi of the Maṇḍala! O Great Cakra Ārya, descend! O Great Cakra Ārya, descend!
On behalf of the Buddha for this night, I, the monk [Name], with single-minded devotion, request you to perform the ritual services (rising,
circumambulating the seats, and reciting the mantra as follows):
Namo siddhārthāya namas tathāgatāya | Takkirāja oṃ vīra vīrakarma mahākāruṇika vajrāgra vajradhara sattva sattva sārathe sārathe trāyase trāyase vidyām ||
Nisambhini darāmarīṣkariye svāhā! May the devas, asuras, yakṣas, and others who have come to listen to the Dharma,
protect the Buddha-dharma with sincere resolve so that it may endure forever,
and each diligently practice the teachings of the World-Honored One.
All you disciples who have come here, whether dwelling upon the earth or in the void,
may you always give rise to a heart of compassion for the world of humans; day and night, may you abide in the Dharma yourselves,
and may all worlds be forever peaceful and secure, benefiting all living beings with boundless merit and wisdom.
All karmic obstacles and hindrances are entirely eliminated; Free from all suffering, one returns to perfect stillness (*parinirvāṇa*).
